extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in NLP/financial text analysis (central bank communication analysts)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and evaluation criteria for sentence-level sentiment analysis of FOMC meeting minutes, including dataset preparation, annotation aspects, model selection, and performance metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-processing pipeline (splitting, stopword removal, filtering, inspection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pre-processing steps used in this study included four main stages: splitting, removing stopwords, filtering for short-length sentences, and inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split longer paragraphs into individual sentences to enable sentence-level analysis; remove stopwords that do not carry significant meaning; filter out sentences too short to be meaningful (typically those with fewer than 8 words or 43 characters); conduct manual inspection to identify errors introduced by automated steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-sentence filtering threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Filter out sentences that were too short to provide meaningful insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically exclude sentences with fewer than 8 words or fewer than 43 characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation aspects (Growth / Employment / Inflation)
rubrics_metrics.description: During labeling, three key aspects of FOMC minutes were considered: Growth, Employment, and Inflation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators assign sentiment labels per aspect (e.g., Growth, Employment, Inflation) because FOMC sentences can convey different sentiments for different economic aspects; use these aspect labels as the basis for 'Actual sentiment' ground truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual annotation as gold standard ('Actual sentiment')
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers meticulously annotated sentences (1,065 sentences) to serve as the 'Actual sentiment' for evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rigorous human labeling, accounting for domain-specific meanings and multiple aspects, as the evaluation benchmark for model comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate/average aspect scores to determine overall sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare model performance, the study computed the average sentiment scores of three aspects and categorized the result as the overall sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Averaging aspect-level sentiment scores (e.g., Growth, Employment, Inflation) can provide a more accurate overall sentiment for sentences where different aspects have different polarities (example: average of -0.33 categorized as Negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model/domain training-data suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Model performance depends on the compatibility between the model's training data and the target domain; FinBERT was trained on datasets like Financial PhraseBank and FiQA and may not be well-suited for FOMC minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether pretraining/fine-tuning corpora reflect the textual style and vocabulary of FOMC minutes; domain mismatch can cause extreme or directionally incorrect predictions (example: FinBERT scoring -0.964 on a sentence interpreted as positive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for FOMC text characteristics (template-based, low emotional content, condensed economic info)
rubrics_metrics.description: FOMC minutes follow templates, avoid expressing emotion, and are highly condensed with dense economic information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design models and preprocessing to handle low affect/emotion, templated phrasing, and compact sentences; expect basic language models to struggle without domain-aware features or contextual matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual matching between syntactic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose 'contextual matching' between nouns and verbs, adjectives and verbs, adverbs and nouns, etc., to better capture language nuances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate methods that match related tokens/phrases (syntactic/semantic relationships) rather than only word-level co-occurrence to capture subtle sentiment cues in economic text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence vs. statement-level context requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence-level sentiment prediction can be insufficient; some sentences require the context of the entire released statement for accurate sentiment interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, evaluate sentences in their broader statement context or supplement sentence-level predictions with statement-level features to improve accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model bias profiling (class and score distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and account for systematic biases in models' score distributions: FinBERT showed a negative/excessively-extreme bias; VADER showed an extremely centered/neutral distribution; GPT-4 produced many 'Neutral' classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect class-wise distributions and tendencies (e.g., skew toward negative or neutral), and consider recalibration, threshold adjustment, or ensembling to mitigate biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral-threshold adjustment for lexicon/rule-based models (VADER)
rubrics_metrics.description: VADER demonstrated a highly centered sentiment distribution; the study allocated a neutral sentiment rate of approximately 10% between -0.05 to 0.05 to enhance classification power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust neutral thresholds for rule-based models (e.g., treat scores between -0.05 and 0.05 as neutral) to better align their output distribution with human-labeled distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use confusion matrix elements for multi-class evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate models using confusion matrices summarizing true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN) for positive/neutral/negative classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report per-class TP/TN/FP/FN counts to understand where models misclassify (e.g., FinBERT strong on negative detection; VADER better at neutral detection but worse on positive/negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: ROC / AUC as performance metric (per class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ROC curves and area under the curve (AUC) to quantify a model's ability to distinguish classes; AUC values reported per class (negative/neutral/positive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret AUC values with domain thresholds (note: Fawcett 2006 suggests AUC >= 0.7 is generally considered good); use per-class AUC (e.g., FinBERT AUC=0.73 for negative class indicates strong negative detection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-class performance interpretation and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Model selection should consider which sentiment class matters most: e.g., FinBERT performed better detecting positive and negative sentiments but worse for neutral; VADER centered on neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose or ensemble models based on class-wise strengths depending on downstream objectives (e.g., prioritize negative-detection if that is most consequential).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of large language models: interpretability and compute/data cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Large language models (e.g., GPT-4) can be hard to interpret and require enormous computing power and data to train; fine-tuning can be opaque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in interpretability, reproducibility, and resource costs when choosing LLMs; supplement LLM outputs with interpretable methods or expert review when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling for representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The study randomly selected 1,065 sentences from 64 FOMC 'Minutes' between 2006/01/03 and 2014/10/08 to form the dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure temporal and document coverage when sampling (random selection across meetings and years) to capture variability in language and avoid selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare multiple models and use ensemble or hybrid approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: The study compares rule-based (VADER), domain-fine-tuned transformers (FinBERT), and LLMs (GPT-4) and suggests combining NLP techniques with statistical models or expert opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically compare models on the human-labeled gold set and consider ensembles or hybrid pipelines (domain-tuned models + statistical methods + human expertise) to overcome individual model limitations.
